title: Cell Natural Orbitals in Interacting Topological Bands
authors: Nishchhal Verma, Harshitra Mahalingam, Daniel Muñoz-Segovia, Raquel Queiroz
abstract: Topological bands exhibit obstruction to exponentially localized and symmetric Wannier functions, challenging the standard paradigm of representing projected interactions in terms of local orbitals with finite range. To faithfully capture the form factors and quantum geometry of topological bands we introduce a singular-value decomposition of the band-projected density form factors, enabling a geometry-based truncation scheme of the Hilbert space, exposing an intrinsic hierarchy on band-projected interactions that is determined by the underlying wavefunctions. This decomposition is most naturally described in terms of Cell Natural Orbitals (CNOs), as the eigenstates of the unit-cell reduced one-particle density matrix, whose occupation provide a measure of the minimal orbital complexity required to faithfully represent the band wavefunctions overlaps. The CNO decomposition identifies systematically the minimal number of local orbitals needed to reproduce short-ranged interactions while resolving the hierarchy of interaction strengths across CNO channels. Applied to magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene in the chiral limit, we find that the dominant CNO is centered at the AA site, resembling the $f$-fermion of the heavy-fermion model. The subdominant CNO channels carry progressively weaker interaction matrix elements, allowing them to be treated at the static mean-field level, while the dominant channel requires a dynamical self-energy. The formalism illustrates how variations of charge density within the unit cell generate momentum dependence in the CNO envelope function and, consequently, dispersion in the single-particle spectral function. More broadly, our results establish CNOs as a geometry-informed bridge between band topology and real-space correlations, providing a systematic framework for analyzing interactions and emergent phases in quantum materials.
summary: This work introduces Cell Natural Orbitals (CNOs) as a powerful tool to bridge momentum-space band theory and real-space correlation physics in topological materials. By decomposing interaction form factors using CNOs, it establishes a systematic hierarchy for treating interactions, allowing researchers to control computational complexity by separating dominant, dynamically coupled channels from weaker, mean-field treatable ones.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of representing interactions in topological bands when standard methods fail due to the non-local nature imposed by band topology.
main_result: Cell Natural Orbitals (CNOs) provide a geometry-informed framework that systematically decomposes projected interactions, revealing an intrinsic hierarchy useful for controlled many-body calculations.
method: The core method involves singular-value decomposition of band-projected density form factors to define CNOs, which are the eigenstates of the unit-cell reduced one-particle density matrix.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to interacting topological materials, specifically using magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene in the chiral limit as a concrete example. The formalism is general for systems exhibiting band topology.
key_observables: CNO occupations (eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix), unit-cell entanglement entropy ($S_{	ext{cell}}$), and the spectral function $A(k, \omega)$.
important_parameters: The relative strength hierarchy between dominant and subdominant CNO channels; momentum dependence in the CNO envelope function.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a geometry-based truncation scheme derived from SVD, and subsequent calculations often employ approximations like the Hubbard-I or Rank-1 approximation for self-energy calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures alongside CNO spectra showing exponential decay, real-space distributions of dominant CNOs (e.g., at AA sites), and evidence of topologically protected zeros in the leading CNO envelope function.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical necessity of CNOs to quantify orbital complexity, demonstrating their utility via entanglement measures ($S_{	ext{cell}}$) in topological phases, and finally applying this framework to calculate self-energies ($\Sigma$) for interacting systems, showing how approximations affect gap closing.
why_interesting: The concept of using natural orbitals derived from a reduced density matrix to systematically truncate the Hilbert space is highly relevant for modeling strongly correlated systems where exact diagonalization is impossible, providing an orbital basis tailored to the underlying band structure topology.
